Hollywood Entertainment invites you to experience a rare 35mm screening of Richard Kwietniowski’s Owning Mahowny on “Brian Molony Day” – the unofficial holiday whose namesake inspired the film’s events.

In one of his most unforgettable yet under-seen performances, Philip Seymour Hoffman immerses you in the double life of Dan Mahowny, a bank employee stealing money from wealthy client accounts to gamble with in Atlantic City and Las Vegas. Casino manager Victor Foss (John Hurt) notices his high rolling and goes out of his way to enable Mahowny’s addiction, flying him and his stolen cash directly to the casinos. Dan’s compulsions cause turmoil with his girlfriend (played by Minnie Driver) and bookie (Maury Chaykin).

The real story: Brian Molony; a CIBC manager who gambled over $10 million (over $34 million today) in stolen funds via mostly sports betting and at Caesars Palace Atlantic City. Because Caesars violated reporting regulations, the state of New Jersey ordered the casino be shut down for a full day. Casino employees deemed that day (November 30, 1985) “Brian Molony Day.”

When Gary Stephen Ross, the author of *Stung: The Incredible Obsession of Brian Molony*, was asked if Hoffman’s portrayal was anything like the real Brian Molony, Ross said, “Philip somehow managed to assimilate the psychic essence of Molony – a yawning emptiness that nothing except gambling was able to fill.”

“Mr. Mahowny would like barbecue ribs- no sauce, and a coke.”

Japanese animation pioneer Noburō Ofuji’s first film, *The Thief of Baguda Castle *premiered on the same bill with Teinosuke Kinugasa’s *A Page of Madness* in 1926. While Kinugasa was advancing live-action cinema, Ofuji introduced his own new stop-motion technique using cut outs of colorfully patterned paper called *chiyogami*. Japanese novelist (and later Nobel Prize winner) Yasunari Kawabata devised the scenario (with contributions from other members of the radical literary movement known as Shinkankakuha) for director Teinosuke Kinugasa’s visionary masterpiece. Believing his wanton cruelty drove his wife insane, a guilt-wracked husband devotes himself to her care as a janitor at the asylum where she’s incarcerated. When it appears her illness may prevent their daughter from getting married, he gradually loses his own grip on reality. Kinugasa’s fantastical images, disorienting super impositions and rapid montage confirmed the expressive power of Japanese silent film. The Archive is honored to premiere this new restoration from the National Film Archive of Japan on the film’s centennial.

The great American filmmaker William Greaves, who in his illustrious career of more than 50 years documented the civil rights movement and historical figures like Muhammad Ali, Paul Robeson, Ida B. Wells, and Raphe Bunche, who executive produced the groundbreaking PBS news program *Black Journal*, and who wrote and directed the radically experimental fiction hybrid *Symbiopsychotaxiplasm*, had one last trick up his sleeve before his death in 2014: He left behind an extraordinary archive of unedited footage from a cocktail party he staged and hosted in 1972 at the home of Duke Ellington, an astonishingly vital and poignant gathering of luminaries from the Harlem Renaissance, many of whom had not seen each other for nearly a half century. Among those assembled were the artists Aaron Douglas and Romare Bearden, the composers Eubie Blake and Noble Sissle, the photographer James Van Der Zee, the poet Arna Bontemps, and the actor Leigh Whipper. Now, some 50 years later, Greaves’ son David, one of three cameramen filming that day, has shaped this never-before-seen material into the beautiful and indelible *Once Upon a Time in Harlem*, carrying on the work of Greaves’ wife and longtime partner Louise Archambault Greaves and collaborating with Greaves’ granddaughter Liani and Anne de Mare as producers.

In a trailblazing entertainment industry career spanning over half a century, producer-director Stan Lathan continues to leave an indelible creative mark. His groundbreaking work in television began with directing the PBS public affairs and documentary series *Say Brother* and *Black Journal*, which were produced to give voice to Black communities following the assassination of Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. Later summoned by Redd Foxx to work on *Sanford and Son* as one of the few Black directors in primetime television, Lathan went on to helm episodes for a wide range of hit series, from *Hill Street Blues* to *Roc*. A formidable talent, he also directed numerous pilots that launched highly successful series, including *Amen* and *Moesha*.

In a career of milestones, following his theatrical feature *Beat Street* (1984), Lathan partnered with Russell Simmons to create *Def Comedy Jam* and *Def Poetry Jam* for HBO, the latter garnering the duo a Peabody Award. Among multiple Emmy, Grammy and Tony Awards and too many other major awards to mention, Lathan was recognized with a CINE Golden Eagle and an American Film Festival Blue Ribbon for directing the *American Playhouse* telefilm *Go Tell It on the Mountain* (1985). In perhaps the highest accolade possible, cultural titan James Baldwin publicly pronounced his love of the TV adaptation of his seminal work.

Join us as we celebrate Stan Lathan with a screening of *Go Tell It on the Mountain*, introduced by NYU Associate Professor Josslyn Luckett.

*Programmed and notes written by John H. Mitchell Television Curator Mark Quigley.*

### **ABOUT THE FILMS:**

**“The First World Festival of Negro Arts,” 1966, Dir. William Greaves, 41 Min, Janus, USA**

Hosted by a newly independent Senegal and overseen by its first president, Léopold Sédar Senghor, throughout April 1966, the First World Festival of Negro Arts showcased dance, music, theater, film and literature from dozens of nations in a historic gathering that encompassed over two thousand attendees, including Langston Hughes, Duke Ellington, Wole Soyinka and Aimé Césaire, among other notable artists and dignitaries. Spotlighting performances from Ethiopia, Trinidad, Chad, Nigeria and several other African and American countries, director William Greaves employs poetic voice-over narration to reflect on the festival’s celebration of Pan-African identity as well as the role that creativity can play in fostering global connection.

FORMAT: DCP

**“Wealth of a Nation,” 1964, Dir. William Greaves, 22 Min, Janus, USA**

Commissioned by the United States Information Agency to produce a documentary on freedom of speech, director William Greaves profiled several artists—including avant-garde sculptor Lee Bontecou, free-jazz trumpeter Bill Dixon and futurist architect William Katavolos—to explore how audacious self-expression can move a society toward higher ideals. Even in this short industrial-film format, Greaves draws on virtuoso camera work and lyrical montage to communicate a signature theme: the deeply reciprocal relationship between creative individuals and their communities.

FORMAT: DCP

**“Booker T. Washington: The Life and the Legacy,” 1985, Dir. William Greaves, 32 Min, Janus, USA**

Infusing fiction with elements of documentary, William Greaves’s short biopic of legendary African American activist Booker T. Washington focuses on how his leadership of the Tuskegee Institute—which equally emphasized practical labor skills and classroom learning—influenced educational philosophy and practice throughout the United States. Screenwriter Lou Potter sets the action during the lifetime of Washington (Maurice Woods), but a modern-day narrator (Gil Noble) interviews the historical personages—and frequently challenges their answers. This experimental format highlights the still-contentious nature of Washington’s political stances, especially his accommodationist strategy for Black integration within the racially hostile South.

FORMAT: DCP

Hell Houses are a distinctly American phenomenon which began in 1990 just outside of Dallas, Texas at the Trinity Assembly of God Church. The original Hell House was conceived as a modern-day fire-and-brimstone sermon. Today, this religious ceremony of sorts is replete with actors, extensive lighting equipment and full audio-visual tech crews.

Inside the Hell House, tour guides dressed as demons take visitors from room to room to view depictions of school massacres, date rape, AIDS-related deaths, fatal drunk driving crashes, and botched abortions. With full access to the behind-the-scenes action, HELL HOUSE follows the process from the first script meeting until the last of the 10,000 visitors passes through the Hell House doors. The movie gives a verite window into the whole process of creating this over-the-top sermon, while showing an intimate portrait of the people who fervently believe its message. Shot on 16mm film and featuring a score by Bubba and Matthew Kadane, formerly of the band Bedhead.

**dir. George Ratliff, 2001**
